..(Tuesday night through Sunday)
Issued at 455 AM EDT MON SEP 7 2026

The extended portion of the forecast remains on track with the
large 5h ridge being shunted south by a stronger northern stream
system Wednesday night through Thursday. The associated sfc front
may be wet enough to support excessive rainfall for parts of the 
area and WPC has upped far eastern Kentucky to a Day 4 Slight 
Risk of excessive rainfall on this account. We will need to keep 
tracking this heavy rain potential during an otherwise benign 
extended forecast period.

The previous long term discussion follows:

When the long term period opens, eastern Kentucky will again find
itself on the eastern fringe of an upper level ridge centered 
over the Mississippi Valley. To the northwest, a closed upper 
level low will be located over southern Saskatchewan. With time, 
the low and its associated trough will translate east, helping to 
flatten the ridge until the forecast area finds itself at the base
of a broad upper level trough late Wednesday into Thursday. Prior
to this, weather will be relatively quiet, with surface high 
pressure located to the east of the forecast area on Tuesday. 
Dewpoints should remain largely in the 60s except perhaps in our 
westernmost counties; thus, although Tuesday will be unseasonably 
hot, with high temperatures in the mid to upper 80s, it will not 
feel as muggy. Overnight, clear skies and a weak pressure gradient
will allow a very modest ridge valley split to develop (on the 
order of a few degrees), with typical valley fog development. 
Moisture will return again Wednesday as the surface high sinks 
south and winds become increasingly southwesterly, bringing 
dewpoints back into the upper 60s or perhaps low 70s in our 
westernmost counties. Highs will again climb into the upper 80s to
perhaps 90 in a few locations. Other than the lingering heat, no 
impactful weather is expected.

The pattern begins to change by Wednesday night as upper level 
troughing digs into the area. A surface cold front extending from 
the now vertically stacked low over Canada will progress toward 
Kentucky through the overnight hours, with rain chances increasing
in northeastern Kentucky as early as Thursday morning. There is 
still some uncertainty regarding the exact timing of this front, 
although ensemble guidance is hinting that rain would most likely 
begin in the late morning or early afternoon for most of the 
forecast area. There is high confidence that this front will 
interact with an anomalously moist air mass; LREF mean PW values 
are in the 1.6-1.8 range, generally representing at least the 80th
percentile compared to climatology. This, plus deterministic 
model soundings showing a deep warm cloud layer, indicates that 
any storms that form could be efficient rain producers capable of 
unleashing torrential downpours. Given this environment, WPC has 
introduced a Day 5 Marginal Risk for Excessive Rainfall for the 
entire forecast area. Thankfully, the progressive nature of this 
system, relatively dry antecedent conditions, and expected fast 
storm motions should work to mitigate the flash flood threat 
somewhat. Additionally, some machine learning guidance has also 
picked up on a low end risk for severe thunderstorms on Thursday, 
and given many deterministic models depict a belt of stronger mid 
level flow just north of the forecast area, it is not 
inconceivable that moderate shear (~30 kts) could support a more 
organized storm mode as the front moves through. Even so, any 
severe risk will remain heavily dependent on frontal timing, and 
with the best shear along and north of the Ohio River, widespread 
severe weather appears implausible at this time.

Model spread increases significantly following the passage of the
cold front. Some deterministic guidance is hinting that an 
additional shortwave trough could spark additional rain chances 
Friday afternoon into Friday night, particularly near the TN and 
VA lines, while other model guidance suggests shortwave ridging 
will build in, keeping the forecast area dry. Similar uncertainty 
exists on Saturday. For now, NBM output has averaged these two 
solutions, resulting in chance PoPs in the southern half of the 
forecast area on Friday and Saturday afternoons, although this 
will bear refining in the future. Ridging looks to build back in 
by the end of the period, marking a return to a drier pattern.
